ports.name: Lisboa
ports.text:
The port at the corner of Europe, where the Atlantic wind system can be used rather than fought. Every Portuguese voyage down the African coast and round to India began here, and the *volta do mar* is what let them come back.

The Armada's muster was taken here on 9 May 1588 — a date often misread as the sailing date. The fleet actually cleared the Tagus on 29–30 May and did not leave Corunna until 22 July.

ports.name: Calicut
rows: arrive Sept, on the SW monsoon
depart Nov–Jan, on the NE monsoon
ports.text:
The far end of the monsoon system, and a working port for fifteen hundred years before any European reached it. The *Periplus* names this coast in the first century AD and gives the month to leave Egypt: July.

Da Gama's arrival in 1498 did not open the route. It connected an Atlantic system to an Indian Ocean one that had been running on schedule for a very long time.
ports.cite: *Periplus Maris Erythraei* §56; Subrahmanyam, *The Career and Legend of Vasco da Gama*.

ports.name: Batavia
rows: from 1619, on the sacked city of Jayakarta
ports.text:
Jayakarta was taken and destroyed in 1619 and rebuilt as the administrative centre of the Dutch East India Company. The port is the reason the passage times on this model are as well known as they are: the VOC counted every voyage, and 8,000 of them survive with dates.

Those records are also why the model can be scored, and why one of its own founding claims had to be corrected — see About.

ports.name: Elmina
ports.text: The oldest European building south of the Sahara, and for three centuries a holding point on the Middle Passage. It is on this map because the *volta do mar* — the piece of wind-field knowledge that makes the whole Atlantic system work — was worked out on the voyages to and from this coast.
ports.cite: Vogt, *Portuguese Rule on the Gold Coast*; Eltis & Richardson.

ports.name: Malacca
ports.text:
The narrowest point on the sea route between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, and therefore continuously fought over for six hundred years. It is still the busiest chokepoint on Earth.

Ships wait here for the monsoon to turn. That has been true since before the port had a name in any European language.
ports.cite: Pires, *Suma Oriental*; US Energy Information Administration, 2024.

ports.name: Roskilde
ports.eyebrow: Port · where the ships were found
rows: five, scuttled c. 1070 to block the fjord
30 m, 60 oars, built in Dublin in 1042 (dendrochronology)
11 kn; the widely quoted 17 kn is an estimate
ports.text:
Five ships were sunk here about 1070 to block a channel, and being sunk is why they survive. Skuldelev 2 was built of Irish oak in Dublin in 1042 — the date and the place both come from tree rings, not from a saga.

Its replica sailed 2,482 nautical miles to Dublin and back. Highest speed actually logged: 13.4 knots over the ground, downwind, in a tidal race. The '17 knots' in circulation is the museum's estimate of a maximum, not a measurement.
ports.cite: Viking Ship Museum, Roskilde, *Thoroughbred of the Sea* (2008).
